analysis.one_liner: Replaces drug patents and market exclusivity with government prize payments for new medicines.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Sanders with zero Senate cosponsors, sat in the Senate health committee for the rest of the Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end the legal monopolies — patents and exclusivity periods — that let brand-name drug companies set high prices for a period of years. Instead of earning money by selling exclusively, the first company to win federal approval for a new drug would get a cash prize from a government fund, and the drug could then be made and sold by any manufacturer at competitive prices. The fund would pay out roughly $100 billion a year (0.55% of GDP), financed by federal appropriations and an annual fee on health insurance companies. It also reserved prize money for neglected diseases, rare diseases, and researchers who share their work openly.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and everyone who pays for medicines. With legal monopolies gone, any manufacturer could make an approved drug immediately, and the bill's stated goal was to radically lower drug prices [S3]. The fund also directs minimum prize money toward diseases of the poor in developing countries, rare (orphan) diseases, and global infectious diseases like AIDS, which market exclusivity often fails to incentivize [S3]. Researchers who openly share knowledge and data on a royalty-free basis would be eligible for prizes too [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, insurers, and taxpayers paying drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates exclusive rights to manufacture, distribute, and sell any drug, biological product, or manufacturing process, ending the price-setting power that comes with monopolies [S3].

Awards prize payments from a new federal fund to the first maker of an approved drug, based on how many patients benefit, the therapeutic improvement over existing treatments, and whether it addresses priority needs like neglected and rare diseases [S2, S3].

Sets minimum shares of fund money for global neglected diseases (at least 4%), orphan diseases (at least 10%), and global infectious diseases including AIDS and bioterrorism countermeasures (at least 4%) [S3].
Dedicates at least 5% of prizes to 'Open Source Dividend' awards for people and communities that openly share knowledge, data, and technology royalty-free [S3].
Requires the government auditor (GAO) to periodically audit whether the prize board is bringing medicines to market cost-effectively and addressing society's medical needs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund about 0.55% of GDP annually for the prize fund — over $100 billion a year by the bill's own findings [S3]. Health insurance companies would also pay an annual fee to help finance the fund, scaled to their premium volume, with smaller insurers (under $25 million in net premiums) exempt [S3]. Brand-name drug companies would give up their exclusive selling rights and would compete for uncertain prize payments instead of guaranteed monopoly profits [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, health insurers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The cost is enormous: 0.55% of GDP in annual federal appropriations — more than $100 billion in a single year by the bill's own estimate — a permanent new federal program financed in part by fees on health insurers that could be passed through to premiums [S3].

The prize system is untested at this scale. Award amounts and selection criteria would be set by a new 13-member board, and prizes are capped at 10 years per product and 5% of the annual fund per product, so innovators face real risk of being under-rewarded compared to monopoly sales — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

Companies currently selling drugs would compete for a shrinking share of prize money in the transition years (only 90% of the 2019 fund could go to existing drugs, then 9% less each year), creating winners and losers among existing treatments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential payoff — generic competition on every medicine, including new ones, driving prices toward production cost — is one of the largest drug-price interventions ever proposed, and it would redirect research incentives toward diseases that monopoly pricing neglects. The costs are also real: a $100-billion-plus annual federal outlay, an unproven prize mechanism run by a new board whose judgments replace market signals, and a transition that would be turbulent for existing drug revenues and patent holders. Whether the fund would actually keep pace with the innovation that patents currently finance is the central open question; the bill itself directs a GAO audit to answer that after the fact [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on March 2, 2017 [S1, S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the Congress [S4].
The committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never received a floor vote, and no further action was ever recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept their patents and exclusive marketing rights — and the monopoly pricing power they fund — because the bill never advanced. Health insurers also avoided the annual fee the bill would have imposed on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept their monopolies

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor throughout the Congress.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat without action after its referral for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred and no other senator cosponsored the bill from either party, so no partisan coalition ever formed on either side [S4, S5].

industries.note: They would lose the patents and exclusivity periods that underpin their pricing power, replaced by competitive prize payments of uncertain size [S3]. Their interest in keeping the current monopoly system runs directly against patients paying drug prices.
They could immediately manufacture any approved drug without waiting for patent or exclusivity periods to expire, expanding their market and driving prices down [S3].

They would pay a new annual fee scaled to premium volume (small insurers exempt), which could push premiums up; on the other hand, sharply lower drug prices would reduce one of their biggest cost drivers [S3].

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug-price intermediaries
industries.note: With no exclusive products to negotiate discounts on, the spreads and rebates these middlemen capture shrink dramatically, since any manufacturer could supply any drug at competitive prices [S3].
